analysis.one_liner: Slashes mercury emissions 95% from power plants, boilers, incinerators, cement plants, and chlor-alkali facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a Democratic and a Republican sponsor, never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate committee it was referred to.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required power plants, industrial boilers, waste incinerators, chlor-alkali chemical plants, and cement plants to cut their mercury emissions by at least 95 percent from a set baseline. It also would have forced manufacturers to label mercury-containing products, phased out the sale of most mercury products unless makers took them back for recycling, and required annual public reporting of each facility's mercury emissions. The stated aim was to reduce mercury that ends up in fish and waterways, which the bill's findings say poses the greatest risk to pregnant women, children, and people who eat a lot of fish.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially pregnant women, children, and communities near coal plants, incinerators, and contaminated waterways. The bill cited EPA data showing 39 states had issued warnings about mercury-tainted fish in 1997, up from 27 in 1993.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each covered facility to cut annual mercury emissions by at least 95 percent from its baseline, with enforceable permits issued within two years
Requires annual public release of facility-specific mercury emission data for every covered power plant, boiler, incinerator, cement plant, and chlor-alkali plant
Phases out sale of mercury-containing products unless the manufacturer proves an essential use, no mercury-free alternative at reasonable cost, and a take-back program
Requires waste handlers to separate and remove mercury items like batteries and fluorescent bulbs from the waste stream, with a preference for recycling over disposal
Funds research on high-risk populations, sets up a public awareness program, and standardizes state fish-consumption advisories

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and oil-fired power plants, industrial boilers, chlor-alkali plants, cement plants, incinerator operators, and makers of mercury-containing products, who would bear the cost of controls, monitoring, labeling, and take-back programs. Some of that cost could pass through to electricity rates and waste-handling fees.

drawbacks.text: The 95 percent reduction mandate is unusually strict; mercury control technology for utility boilers was not fully proven at the time, and compliance could raise electricity and waste-disposal costs for consumers
The product ban could remove some mercury-containing goods from the market, softened only by exemptions for essential uses with no reasonable alternative
Waste haulers and solid waste facilities would have to submit and implement approved plans within months, an administrative burden for smaller operators

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are large: mercury is a neurotoxin, and the bill's own findings note a steep rise in fish-consumption advisories. The costs fall on a small set of industries and could partially pass to consumers in electricity and waste fees, but the bill allows site-level emissions trading and flexible control methods, which is a reasonable cost-containment design. On balance the public health benefit outweighs the cost, though the strict 95 percent figure leaves little room for facilities facing genuinely unproven technology.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the bill for himself and Sen. Olympia Snowe on March 19, 1999, giving it one sponsor from each party
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal- and oil-fired power plants, mercury-cell chlor-alkali plants, cement makers, and incinerator operators were better off, because no 95 percent emission cuts, permits, or public reporting requirements were ever imposed.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction under Chairman John Chafee (R-RI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die in committee

sides.party_line_note: The record shows a bipartisan introduction, one Democrat and one Republican, but no votes or recorded opposition, so the partisan shape of the outcome cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill names fossil-fuel power plants as the largest U.S. source of mercury emissions and would require 95 percent cuts, permits, monitoring, and public reporting. The EPA report cited in the bill links their emissions to methyl mercury in fish, the main route of human exposure.
These chemical plants use mercury directly in production and would face the same 95 percent reduction mandate. Their emissions are an avoidable byproduct of an older production process.
Cement kilns would face 95 percent cuts in direct and fugitive mercury dust emissions plus permitting and reporting. The bill carves out emissions already regulated as hazardous-waste burning.

industries.industry: Solid waste and medical waste incineration
industries.note: Incinerators would face a maximum mercury emission rate, mandatory control equipment if they exceed it, and monitoring rules. Municipal incinerators are a major pathway for mercury from discarded consumer products.

A three-year phaseout would bar sales of mercury-containing products, including batteries and fluorescent bulbs, unless the maker wins an exemption proving essential use and a take-back program. Labeling and waste-separation duties also fall on manufacturers and waste handlers.
